name: PT Multi Bintang Indonesia Tbk

frontmatter.title: Multi Bintang Indonesia: a fully distributed cash machine priced for decline
frontmatter.summary: Multi Bintang is the Indonesian beer platform of Heineken, and its 2026 recovery is operating rather than accounting: nine-month sales and operating profit both stepped up on volume, price and premium mix. The shares pay out essentially all earnings, yield 10.8% on our forecast and trade at 9.2x earnings, a price that implies decline. We initiate at BUY.
thesis: The 2026 recovery is real and sourced: nine-month net sales of Rp2,877.8bn against Rp2,368.5bn, and operating profit of Rp1,159.7bn against Rp935.0bn, with gross profit up on volume, price and premium mix [S10].
Essentially all earnings are distributed: FY2025 dividends of Rp561 per share against EPS of Rp562, a payout of 99.9%, and the shares yield 10.8% on our FY2026E forecast [S8].
The dividend is not levered: the group carries net cash of Rp-875.7bn after repaying its bank facility during 2026, and working capital is structurally negative [S10].

The market pays 9.2x forward earnings for a franchise we value at Rp8,837; the reverse DCF solves a parallel five-point cut to revenue growth in every forecast year, taking FY2027E growth to 1.0% and the terminal rate below zero [S0].
The binding constraint is liquidity and policy, not solvency: a 9.6% free float and IDR588.9m of daily turnover justify the 10.00% liquidity discount in our target [S0].

catalysts.event: Interim dividend for FY2026 expected to be declared and paid in December, following the FY2025 pattern
Government decision on excise tariffs for 2027, the single largest swing factor in the earnings model
FY2026 audited results and the final dividend proposal to the annual general meeting; the free-float step to twelve-and-a-half per cent also falls due, a dated Heineken sell-down
First-quarter 2027 interim financial statements, the first test of whether the recovery annualises

blocks.text: We initiate coverage of Multi Bintang Indonesia with a BUY and a twelve-month target of Rp7,274 per share, 16.4% above the Rp6,250 last price and a total return of 27.2% once the Rp675 of dividends we expect over the next twelve months is added [S0]. The target is the weighted value of Rp8,082 after the 10.00% discount the house applies to a name this tightly held, and it sits below our DCF value of Rp8,837 because the target passes through the probability-weighted scenarios, including a bear case the DCF does not carry, and then the illiquidity discount [S0].

The market is pricing an annuity in run-off. At 9.2x forward earnings and 5.4x forward EBITDA the shares discount a business that has already demonstrated the opposite: nine-month net sales of Rp2,877.8bn against Rp2,368.5bn a year earlier and operating profit of Rp1,159.7bn against Rp935.0bn, with gross profit rising to Rp1,794.0bn on a wider base [S10]. The company did not buy that growth with margin: the gross margin held at 64.2% and the operating margin at 43.9% on our full-year forecast, which is the last actual economics, not a heroic recovery [S10].

Our variant view is that the 2025 weakness was cyclical and policy-driven rather than structural, and that the market has extrapolated it. The company itself attributed the soft market to lower-than-expected category growth [S9]; what followed was a nine-month rebound across both the alcoholic and the non-alcoholic portfolio [S10]. Because the payout is essentially all of earnings, and because the balance sheet holds net cash rather than debt [S10], the value of the equity is the value of a growing stream of distributions, and a mid-single-digit growth rate on a double-digit cost of equity is worth far more than Rp6,250 [S0].

A total return of this size has to be named rather than asserted, and three sourced drivers produce it. First, the FY2026E revenue base of Rp4,194.4bn is not a forecast from thin air: it annualises the nine-month actual with a slower fourth quarter [S10]. Second, the cost structure is held at the rates the last actual year actually paid, a gross margin of 64.2% and an operating-cost ratio of 20.3%, both anchored on reported figures rather than on a hoped-for operating leverage [S9]. Third, the payout of 99.9% converts those earnings into cash in the shareholders' hands, and the shares yield 10.8% on that basis [S8]. The discount rate that ties them together is 12.0%, which carries a premium for control and single-country alcohol regulation but not for illiquidity, which is charged separately [S0]. What today's price implies, if our cost of capital is right, is a parallel cut of about five points to revenue growth in every year of the forecast, FY2027E growth of 1.0% against the 6.0% we forecast and a terminal rate below zero — a business in perpetual decline, not one weak year [S0].

Multi Bintang is the Indonesian operating platform of the Heineken group: it brews, markets and distributes beer and a smaller range of non-alcoholic beverages, and it has been listed on the Indonesian exchange since 1981 [S9]. The operating footprint is a brewery in Tangerang and a non-alcoholic beverages plant in Sampangagung, with distribution run through a dedicated subsidiary, PT Multi Bintang Indonesia Niaga, which employed its own staff and operated as the group's main beverage distributor [S10]. Group headcount is small for the revenue base — 414 persons direct employees at the end of FY2025 and 417 persons at the end of the third quarter of 2026 — because brewing is capital-intensive and the distribution model leans on third-party wholesalers [S9].

The revenue mix is overwhelmingly alcoholic. FY2025 net sales of Rp3,542.5bn split into Rp3,294.0bn of alcoholic products and Rp248.5bn of non-alcoholic products, and the two moved in opposite directions: alcoholic sales grew while the non-alcoholic range, which had been built around a dedicated plant, contracted [S9]. That mix matters for the valuation because the alcoholic portfolio carries the pricing power and the excise exposure, while the non-alcoholic range carries neither and has been the drag on reported growth [S7]. The portfolio is built on the Bintang brand and its line extensions, including the low-alcohol Radler variant launched from the Sampangagung plant, together with the Heineken brand itself, which the company supports with draught-quality programmes in key outlets [S9].

Strategically the company is doing three things at once. It is premiumising, pushing draught and higher-margin serves through on-premise outlets, which is where the Heineken draught training programme sits [S9]. It is widening the portfolio rather than the geography, using Radler and the non-alcoholic range to reach occasions that beer alone does not serve [S9]. And it is testing exports at the margin: a first shipment of canned Radler to Australia was reported in 2026 and export revenue grew strongly, but exports remain a fraction of a percent of consolidated sales, part of it to related parties [S8]. None of these is large enough to move the group on its own; together they are the difference between a volume-led brewer and a brand-led one.

Multi Bintang is the leader in the legal beer segment, and its position rests on scale in a market where the fixed costs of brewing, excise administration and cold-chain distribution are high relative to the size of the category [S9]. The controlling shareholder is Heineken International B.V. with 89.3% of the shares; the public holds the rest, and the free float available to trade is only 9.6% of the company [S9]. That ownership structure is the defining fact of the investment: it gives the company access to a global brewer's brands, technology and procurement, and it simultaneously means that minority holders own a small, illiquid slice of a subsidiary whose capital allocation is decided elsewhere [S0].

The group structure is simple: the listed entity owns the breweries and the distribution subsidiary, with only a sliver of non-controlling interest in the subsidiary that runs the non-alcoholic plant [S9]. There are no material holdings outside the operating business, no listed associates to value separately and no conglomerate discount to argue about. What the shareholder owns is a brewery, a brand portfolio licensed from its parent, a distribution arm and a net cash balance, and the valuation treats it as exactly that [S9].

The Indonesian beer market is small per head and highly taxed, which is why its history is one of long plateaus punctuated by policy shocks rather than of steady compounding. FY2025 was one of the weak years: the company's own review says the beer market grew by less than it had projected, with consumer purchasing power under pressure and a trade-down into cheaper and untaxed alternatives [S9]. The nine months to September 2026 reversed that, with consolidated net sales of Rp2,877.8bn against Rp2,368.5bn and operating profit of Rp1,159.7bn against Rp935.0bn, a recovery the company attributes to higher volume, effective pricing and portfolio performance [S8].

Excise is the industry's dominant variable. The government sets the tariff annually, and the FY2025 annual report records that the framework for 2026 left the tariff unchanged, with the possibility of an increase in a later year if the economy does not clear the growth threshold the regulation sets [S9]. That single decision moves volume, price and mix simultaneously: a tariff increase forces a price increase, the price increase compresses volume, and the company absorbs part of it in margin to protect share [S9]. The other regulatory layers — the legal drinking age, regional restrictions on where alcohol may be sold, and the advertising code — matter less for earnings in any single year but shape the size of the addressable market over time [S9].

Competition in the legal segment is concentrated. Multi Bintang is the largest player, and the challengers are a small number of national and regional brewers plus imported brands at the premium end [S9]. The more important competitor is untaxed and illicit product, which is why the company's industry commentary dwells on excise disparity and enforcement rather than on price wars with named rivals [S9]. In a market where the legal product carries a large tax wedge, the cheapest competitor is the one that pays no tax, and enforcement is therefore a commercial variable rather than a legal footnote.

On the five forces, the picture is mixed but favourable to the incumbent. Rivalry among legal brewers is moderate because the category is concentrated and price competition destroys excise-adjusted margin for everyone [S9]. The threat of new entry is low: brewing licences, distribution reach and the capital cost of a brewery are real barriers, and the brand that dominates the category is not replicable with capital alone [S9]. Buyer power is low at the consumer level but concentrated at the distributor level, where two customers each take more than a tenth of consolidated sales [S7]. Supplier power is moderate, because malt, hops and packaging are globally priced and the group buys through its parent, and the substitute threat is high in the form of untaxed alcohol and other beverage categories [S9].

The moat is the brand plus the route to market. Bintang is the reference beer of the category, and the company reinforces it with draught quality programmes in outlets, which raise the cost of displacement for a bar or restaurant [S9]. Scale in brewing and excise administration spreads fixed costs over a large base, and the parent's procurement and technical support lower input cost and improve consistency [S9]. What the moat does not protect against is policy: a tariff increase applies to the whole legal market and the incumbent cannot escape it, which is why the bear case is a policy case rather than a competitive one [S9].

Indonesian brewing began in the colonial period, when Dutch and other European brewers built plants to serve expatriate and urban demand, and the industry has always been shaped more by the state's revenue appetite than by competition between brands. Beer has never been the mass-market drink of the archipelago; the category sits alongside tea, coffee and palm-based drinks, and its consumption is concentrated among urban, younger and tourist-facing consumers. That history explains the structure of the modern market: a small number of licensed brewers, heavy fixed costs, a dominant national brand, and a tax regime that treats alcohol as a revenue source and a social problem at the same time.

The external influences that matter most for the next two years are tourism, purchasing power and the currency. Bali and the other tourist destinations are a disproportionate part of premium and draught volume, so the tourism cycle shows up in mix before it shows up in total sales [S9]. Purchasing power determines whether the trade-down into cheaper and untaxed product continues [S9]. And the rupiah matters because malt, hops and much of the packaging are priced in dollars: at the deck's forward rate of Rp18,350 per dollar, against Rp18,004 spot, the imported share of cost of goods is a live margin variable, and the company reported a net foreign-exchange loss in the nine months that sits just below the operating line [S10]. The model reads no FX driver because the decks carry no barley, hops or glass series; instead the gross margin carries the full cost path, and the FY2026E margin is held at the last actual level rather than credited with any rupiah benefit [S10].

FY2025 was a flat year at the top and a slightly better one at the bottom. Revenue of Rp3,542.5bn grew 4.7%, gross profit reached Rp2,258.8bn at a 63.8% margin, operating profit was Rp1,534.1bn and net profit attributable to shareholders was Rp1,183.3bn, a margin of 33.4% [S9]. The mix told the real story: alcoholic sales grew, the non-alcoholic range fell sharply, and the company still held its gross margin, which is the signature of price and mix discipline rather than volume leverage [S7].

The nine months to September 2026 are the evidence that the model works when the market cooperates. Net sales rose to Rp2,877.8bn, gross profit to Rp1,794.0bn, operating profit to Rp1,159.7bn and net profit to Rp898.0bn, all against the prior-year comparatives in the same filing [S10]. Selling expenses grew faster than sales as the company reinvested in the recovery, and a net foreign-exchange loss sat between operating profit and pre-tax profit; neither changes the shape of the year [S10]. We forecast FY2026E revenue of Rp4,194.4bn, operating profit of Rp1,841.3bn and attributable profit of Rp1,426.3bn, which annualises the nine-month run rate with a deliberately slower fourth quarter [S10].

The restatement that matters is depreciation. The data pack's depreciation charge for FY2025 is a small fraction of the real one because the Indonesian cash-flow statement is presented on the direct method; the notes allocate Rp283.8bn of depreciation and amortisation in FY2025 and Rp288.3bn in FY2024, split between manufacturing overhead and general and administrative expense [S9]. We rebuild history from those figures, which lifts EBITDA to Rp1,817.9bn and an EBITDA margin of 51.3% [S0]. Every cash-cost and leverage ratio in this report uses the restated charge; the pack's version would have overstated cash conversion and understated the capital intensity of the business [S9].

Capital expenditure is maintenance-led. FY2025 spending on property, plant, equipment and right-of-use assets was Rp211.0bn, or 6.0% of revenue, below the restated depreciation charge [S9]. That is the pattern of a company whose capacity is already built: the Tangerang brewery and the Sampangagung plant are in place, and the capital programme is replacement and efficiency rather than expansion [S9]. We hold capital expenditure at 6.0% of revenue, below depreciation, which is why free cash flow exceeds accounting profit even before working capital [S0]. That gap cannot persist through the terminal value: from FY2031E we step capex up to 13.0% of revenue, above the 8.0% depreciation charge, so that the later growth is funded by reinvestment rather than assumed free [S9].

Working capital is a source of cash, not a use. Trade payables, excise and promotional accruals and container deposits exceed receivables and inventory, leaving operating working capital of Rp-1,032.0bn on a growing revenue base, a negative balance of roughly -29.0% of sales [S9]. Growth therefore releases a little cash each year instead of absorbing it, and the container-deposit liability behaves like a customer float [S9]. The one divergence is receivables, and it is not benign. Third-party trade receivables rose from Rp439.3bn to Rp547.1bn while revenue grew 4.7%, so receivables grew several times faster than the top line [S9]. We used to read that as distributor credit without a cash cost; the cash-flow statement does not support it. Operating cash flow fell to Rp1,415.1bn from Rp1,861.6bn, days sales outstanding lengthened by roughly a week and a half, and cash conversion deteriorated even as reported profit rose [S9]. We record this in the disconfirming facts as an optics-class flag — extended distributor terms in a weak volume year, disclosed rather than hidden — not as channel stuffing: the balances are third-party trade receivables carried at cost, the nine-month recovery is corroborated by gross profit and operating profit rather than by sales alone, and the major-customer relationships are disclosed [S9][S10]. A second year of receivables outrunning revenue would move the classification and is on the monitoring list.

Cash generation remains the strongest part of the record, but it weakened in FY2025. Net cash from operations was Rp1,415.1bn against attributable profit of Rp1,183.3bn, so the accruals ratio is still negative — earnings ran behind cash rather than ahead of it, the opposite of the warning sign the quality screen looks for [S9]. The cushion is thinner than a year earlier, when operating cash flow was Rp1,861.6bn on a smaller profit; the deterioration is the receivables build set out above, not a change in the payables or inventory profile, and it is why we carry the divergence as an optics-class flag rather than explain it away. Free cash flow to the firm was Rp1,236.9bn after the restated depreciation and the maintenance capital programme [S0]. The balance sheet carries Rp982.6bn of cash against Rp106.9bn of debt, almost all of it lease liabilities, for net cash of Rp-875.7bn; the short-term bank facility was repaid during 2026 and stood at nil at the end of September [S10].

Capital allocation is simple and, for a minority holder, both the attraction and the risk: the company pays out essentially everything. FY2025 dividends totalled Rp561 per share, an interim and a final, or Rp1,180.0bn against attributable profit of Rp1,183.3bn, a payout of 99.9% [S8]. The equity base is therefore small, with book value per share of Rp644, and the return on it is correspondingly high at 88.5%, which says more about distribution policy than about incremental returns on capital [S0]. There is no buyback, no treasury stock and no change in the share count [S9].

Our forecast is deliberately unheroic after FY2026E. Revenue growth fades from 18.4% to 6.0%, then to 4.5% and 3.0% by the end of the explicit horizon, which is price plus mix with volume roughly flat in a mature category [S9]. The gross margin holds at 64.2% and drifts up with premium mix, the operating-cost ratio stays at 20.3%, and the effective tax rate is 23.5%, the rate the last actual year paid [S9]. Earnings per share reach Rp677 in FY2026E and Rp764 in FY2028E, with dividends of Rp675 and Rp762 respectively [S0].

The earnings-quality screens are clean on most tests, with one optics-class flag. Accruals are still negative and cash conversion is still above one, but both moved the wrong way in FY2025: operating cash flow fell while attributable profit rose, and days sales outstanding lengthened, which is the receivables item above rather than a provisioning or inventory issue [S9]. There is no PSAK 16 revaluation uplift in the property, plant and equipment balance, which is carried at cost [S9], and the shares carry no special notation or special-monitoring-board status that we could find in the filings or the exchange record [S0]. Related-party flows are modest: royalty, technical, management and procurement charges to the Heineken group were Rp25.7bn in FY2025 against Rp16.6bn in FY2024, small relative to revenue of Rp3,542.5bn, and export sales to related parties were Rp6.7bn [S9]. The concentration that we do flag is customer concentration: the largest customer took Rp790.4bn of nine-month sales and Rp992.0bn in FY2025, and a second distributor also exceeds a tenth of consolidated sales, both disclosed as major customers rather than as related parties [S10].

The disconfirming facts we carry into the valuation are these. First, the trade-receivables build: third-party receivables rising several times faster than revenue with operating cash flow down on the year is an optics-class earnings-quality flag, not a manipulation-class one, because the revenue recovery is corroborated below the sales line and the balances are disclosed third-party trade debt [S9][S10]. Second, the non-alcoholic range contracted in FY2025 even as the alcoholic portfolio grew, so the portfolio-widening part of the strategy was not working before the 2026 rebound [S9]. Third, the category itself did not grow as the company expected in FY2025, with trade-down to untaxed alternatives, which is the evidence against a widening moat and the reason the DCF fades terminal growth to price-only [S9]. We do not treat any of these as manipulation-class, and none changes the rating; they are the tests a BUY has to survive, and the receivables trend is the one that would kill it if repeated.

We value Multi Bintang primarily on a discounted cash flow to the firm, with price-to-earnings (P/E) and EV/EBITDA cross-checks. The method fits the business: it is capital-intensive, carries no meaningful debt, distributes essentially all of its earnings, and has a single operating segment with a visible cost structure, the conditions under which a cash-flow model is more informative than a book-value or sum-of-the-parts approach [S9]. The compounder method card that governs this name also demands that we value the distributions rather than the accounting earnings, because the payout is the return [S8].

The cost of capital is built from the house macro deck with a premium we add for the specific risks of this security, and the arithmetic is shown in full because a cost of equity a reader cannot reproduce is a cost of equity a reader should not trust. The engine starts from the Indonesian risk-free rate of 7.4%, deducts the sovereign default spread of 1.6% it carries on that proxy so that the risk-free rate and the equity risk premium sit on the same government curve, then adds the industry beta of 0.70 times the sum of the mature-market equity risk premium of 4.2% and the country risk premium of 2.5%, and finally adds our company premium of 1.5% [S0]. That gives a cost of equity of 12.0%, and with debt at 0.2% of capital the weighted cost is 12.0% [S0]. The premium compensates for two risks the beta cannot see: a single-country regulatory regime for alcohol and a controlling shareholder who sets dividend policy [S9]. A thin free float is deliberately not in it: illiquidity is charged once, through the separate liquidity discount on the target, and building it into the discount rate as well would double count the same risk. At 12.0% the cost of equity sits inside the band the compounder card sets for Indonesian consumer franchises, not at its top end [S0].

The explicit forecast runs to FY2035E in two fade stages: growth falls from 6.0% to 4.5% and then to 4.0% and finally 3.0% [S0]. The terminal value is therefore 41.4% of enterprise value, a smaller share than a flat perpetuity would produce and what we would expect for a mature brewer whose terminal growth is price-only [S0]. Terminal growth of 3.0% is below the nominal GDP growth the macro deck implies and below every explicit-year rate, and it is reconciled to reinvestment rather than declared. Terminal capex of 13.0% of revenue against a 8.0% depreciation charge, plus the small working-capital release, is a net reinvestment rate of about twelve per cent of NOPAT, so 3.0% growth implies an incremental return on invested capital near twenty-five per cent — still twice the cost of capital, but a long way below the historical implied return, which is the fade the compounder card requires [S0][S9]. On those inputs the DCF produces an enterprise value of Rp17,428.5bn and an equity value of Rp8,837 per share [S0].

The cross-checks disagree, and the disagreement is the investment case, but the comparison has to be on a common basis. The engine's P/E cross-check applies the peer median of 9.7 to trailing FY2025A attributable profit of Rp1,183.3bn, giving Rp5,475, -38.0% below the DCF; the EV/EBITDA cross-check applies 7.7 to trailing FY2025A EBITDA of Rp1,817.9bn, giving Rp7,235, -18.1% below it [S0]. Both are trailing figures and the peer median is trailing too, so the like-for-like comparison is MLBI's trailing P/E of 11.1x against the 9.7 peer median — a premium, not the discount that a forward-versus-trailing comparison would suggest [S0]. On our FY2026E earnings the shares trade at 9.2x, and the same peer median applied to FY2026E attributable profit of Rp1,426.3bn would produce a value above the current price but still below our target; the apparent forward discount is mostly the gap between our forward earnings and a peer set measured on trailing ones, and we do not claim it as margin of safety [S0]. Two further things explain why the peer multiples sit below the DCF at all. First, the peer set has de-rated: premium consumer franchises on this exchange no longer trade at the multiples they carried before the current cycle, and a trailing multiple on a de-rated sector will always sit below a DCF that prices the distributions [S0]. Second, a single-year multiple ignores the terminal value and the payout: the shares yield 10.8% on our forecast, and the growth after the explicit horizon, even after the fade, is a large part of the DCF [S0]. We therefore weight the DCF at 60%, the earnings multiple at 30% and the EBITDA multiple at 10% — the industry template's default weighting, unchanged, because the multiples are cross-checks of a de-rated peer set and not independent valuations [S0]. We use the peer median rather than the company's own history for those cross-checks, precisely because the own-history multiple still reflects the pre-de-rating era [S0].

The relative-value test is uncomfortable and we state it plainly. Our target of Rp7,274 sits above the 9.2x at which the shares trade today on FY2026E earnings of 676.9 per share, and above a peer median of 9.7 — the re-rating is part of the call. But on a like-for-like trailing basis the shares already trade at 11.1x against the 9.7 peer median, a premium, and the peer-median cross-check on trailing earnings (Rp5,475) is well below the current price; applied to our FY2026E earnings the same multiple would sit above the current price but still below the target [S0]. On the one method that measures what comparable Indonesian consumer names actually trade at, there is no margin of safety on the trailing comparison and only a thin one on the forward comparison. The BUY therefore does not rest on the peer test; it rests on the DCF, and the premium to the peer median has to be earned by returns and distribution rather than by the multiple itself: MLBI converts essentially all earnings into dividends, pays out 99.9% of attributable profit, and earns a book return on equity of 88.5%, which is why a trailing P/E comparison by itself understates the cash return [S8]. If the board ever cut the payout, the peer-median test would become the binding one and the rating would not survive it.

The multiple-survival test is quantified rather than asserted. The terminal value is 41.4% of the enterprise value of Rp17,428.5bn, which over FY2035E EBITDA of Rp3,130.0bn is an exit EV/EBITDA of about six and a half times and an exit EV/EBIT of under eight times, against an entry of 5.4x on FY2026E EBITDA [S0]. That is still some multiple expansion and we say so: the DCF needs the market to pay a normal multiple for a mature brewer at exit. It is no longer the roughly nine-times exit that a no-fade, no-reinvestment perpetuity implied, because terminal capex now exceeds depreciation and pays for the growth. On reinvestment, capex rises from 6.0% of revenue in the explicit years to 13.0% in the terminal year against a 8.0% depreciation charge; the gap plus the working-capital release is net investment of about twelve per cent of NOPAT, so terminal growth is manufactured by reinvestment at an incremental return near twenty-five per cent rather than assumed free [S9]. We do not fade the reported return on equity, which stays near 91.5% because the company distributes essentially all earnings and keeps book equity small; that is a distribution artefact, not a claim that new capital earns the book return. The return that matters for the DCF is the incremental return on invested capital, and the fade is stated there: the historical implied return is so high that FY2025 fixed assets of Rp1,333.4bn are largely offset by negative working capital of Rp-1,032.0bn, leaving invested capital a small fraction of the operating profit of Rp1,534.1bn it supports, and we fade the terminal incremental return to twenty-five per cent [S9]. That is why the target sits below the DCF and why we apply a liquidity discount: the blended value of Rp8,082 is reduced by 10.00% for a stock whose three-month average daily turnover is IDR588.9m, small enough that a position of any size cannot be exited at the screen price [S0].

The sensitivity table shows what the target is really a bet on: the cost of equity and the terminal growth rate, not the near-term earnings. A hundred-basis-point increase in the cost of capital takes the DCF down by about eight per cent, and a hundred-basis-point increase in terminal growth takes it up by about five per cent; the table shows both, and neither is enough to close the gap to Rp6,250 unless growth turns negative in perpetuity [S0]. That is the point of the reverse DCF: the engine solves a uniform shift applied to revenue growth in every forecast year, so today's price implies roughly a five-point cut to growth throughout the horizon — FY2027 revenue growth of 1.0% against our 6.0%, and a terminal rate below zero — a business that declines for a decade rather than one that has a weak single year, and we do not think that is the most likely path [S0].

The dominant risk is excise policy, and it is a risk we cannot diversify away. The government sets the tariff annually, and although the 2026 framework left it unchanged, the regulation allows an increase if the economy does not clear the growth threshold it sets [S9]. A tariff increase is passed into price, price compresses volume, and the company absorbs part of the effect in margin to defend share; the bear case is simply that this happens in 2027 and again in 2028 [S9]. Likelihood is high over a multi-year horizon and impact is high, which is why the stock has de-rated and why we treat the excise decision as the first item on the monitoring list [S9].

The second risk is the consumer. The FY2025 experience showed how quickly the category stalls when purchasing power weakens and consumers trade down into cheaper and untaxed alternatives [S9]. Beer is discretionary, and in a market where the legal product carries a large tax wedge, a weak consumer does not merely drink less; they drink something else [S9]. The third is currency and input cost: malt, hops and packaging are globally priced, and the rupiah's level feeds directly into cost of goods; the company reported a net foreign-exchange loss below the operating line in the nine months, a reminder that the exposure is real even when it is not in gross margin [S10].

Operationally, concentration is the exposure. Beer is brewed at a small number of sites, and the Tangerang brewery carries most of the volume; an interruption there would be material [S9]. Governance carries the usual risk of a controlled company: with 89.3% held by Heineken, minority holders cannot change strategy, capital allocation or dividend policy, and the related-party charges for royalty, technical and procurement services of Rp25.7bn are set within the group [S9]. Liquidity is the fourth risk and the one that shapes the target, and it is not only a matter of judgment: the exchange registry records a free float of 9.6% against a minimum of fifteen per cent, so the company sits below the threshold and must step up to twelve-and-a-half per cent by the end of March 2027 and to fifteen per cent a year later [S0]. That step is a dated supply event, not a hypothetical: it requires Heineken to place roughly sixty-one million shares, about IDR588.9m of daily turnover for more than six hundred trading days' worth of average volume, and a seller of that size will clear at a discount to the screen price [S0]. It is why a 10.00% discount is applied to the target and why the bear case assumes the placement clears at a wider one [S0].

Our scenarios mirror each other on the same two drivers and the probabilities sum to one. In the bear case, with probability 25.0%, the recovery proves cyclical, excise rises again in 2027 and the premium and tourist volume fades, taking revenue growth four points below base and the gross margin two points lower; the free-float placement then clears into that weaker tape, which is the supply event the report has to carry; that produces a value of Rp6,323 [S9]. In the bull case, with probability 25.0%, the tariff stays frozen, tourism and the premium and non-alcoholic portfolios keep taking share, and operating leverage on a fixed brewery base lifts the margin by the same two points on four points more growth, producing Rp10,175 [S9]. The bull case also carries the float: a sell-down to the threshold removes the overhang and restores index eligibility, which would let us remove the whole 10.00% discount, and a sustained recovery in the non-alcoholic range — which grew by more than a third in the nine months to Rp230.4bn from Rp169.4bn after falling in FY2025 — is worth more of the earnings base than the model gives it [S10]. The base case, at 50.0%, holds the last actual economics and produces Rp7,915 [S0].

The signposts that would change our view are specific. A 2027 excise increase above inflation, or a regional restriction on off-premise alcohol sales, would move us toward the bear case [S9]. Two consecutive quarters of negative volume growth with a stable excise regime would say the issue is demand rather than policy [S10]. A payout cut, or a decision to retain cash for an acquisition, would remove the reason we own the shares [S8]. Conversely, a second year of frozen excise with the non-alcoholic range growing again would justify moving toward the bull case, and any increase in the free float, such as a parent sell-down, would let us remove part of the liquidity discount [S0].

Control sits in Amsterdam. Heineken International B.V. holds 89.3% of the shares, the public holds the remainder, and the free float is 9.6% of the company [S9]. The board is led by a president director appointed from within the group, and the supervisory board is constituted under Indonesian company law with commissioners including group nominees [S9]. For a minority holder the practical consequence is that the dividend is a group decision: the payout of essentially all earnings is generous today, but it is a policy rather than a contractual right, and it can change with the parent's own capital needs [S8].

Related-party dealings are disclosed and mostly structural. The group pays Heineken entities for royalty, technical, management and procurement services, Rp25.7bn in FY2025 against Rp16.6bn in FY2024, and exports a small amount to related parties, Rp6.7bn in FY2025 [S9]. Those charges are a fraction of revenue and are disclosed line by line, which is the standard this market should be held to; they are also the channel through which value could be moved without minority consent, so the ratio is worth watching each year [S9]. We found no pledge of the controlling shareholding and no special notation or monitoring-board status attached to the shares [S0].

The audit is done by Siddharta Widjaja & Rekan, and the FY2025 financial statements carry an unmodified opinion [S9]. The dividend record is the strongest part of the governance story: the company has paid out at double-digit yields in recent years and has raised the dividend with earnings rather than funding it from reserves [S8]. Property, plant and equipment is carried at cost with no revaluation uplift, so book value is not flattered and the price-to-book multiple of 8.2x is a real multiple of real capital rather than of a revalued asset [S9].

ESG exposures are those of a brewer. Water is the material input and the material local externality, and the sustainability report addresses water use at the brewery level [S9]. Packaging is the second: glass is heavy, returnable bottles and container deposits are part of the operating model, the deposit liability is a real balance-sheet item, and the company reports on lightweighting and returnable packaging [S9]. Alcohol responsibility is the third and the one that carries regulatory risk: marketing codes, drink-driving enforcement and regional sales restrictions all bear on the addressable market, and the company's sustainability reporting covers responsible marketing [S9]. Illicit trade is an ESG issue as well as a commercial one, because untaxed alcohol undercuts the legal market and undermines the excise base the state depends on [S9].

The dated catalysts are the dividend and the excise decision. Following the FY2025 pattern, an interim dividend for FY2026 should be declared and paid in December, and the FY2026 final will be proposed at the annual general meeting with the audited results [S8]. The government's excise decision for 2027 is due around the turn of the year and is the single largest swing factor in the earnings model [S9]. The first-quarter 2027 interim statements, due in April, are the first test of whether the nine-month recovery annualises or fades against a strong comparative [S10]. The dated supply catalyst sits at the end of that quarter: the free-float step to twelve-and-a-half per cent falls due on 31 March 2027, and how Heineken places the stock — a marketed block, a strategic buyer or an index-driven selldown — determines whether the liquidity discount narrows or the price takes the discount instead [S0].

Between updates we watch five things. Volume and mix, because price-led growth and volume-led growth have different durability [S10]. The gross margin, because it is where excise and input costs land before they reach operating profit [S9]. The operating-cost ratio, because the nine months showed selling expenses growing faster than sales [S10]. Trade receivables, because they grew faster than revenue in FY2025 and a second year of that would change how we read the cash conversion [S9]. And the payout, because the investment case is the distribution: any move away from paying out essentially all earnings would force us to re-underwrite the name, not merely trim the target [S8].

bear.narrative: The 2026 recovery proves cyclical rather than structural: excise is raised again in 2027, the tourism and festive volume fades, and the company has to spend to hold share in a shrinking legal beer market. Revenue growth falls 4 points below base and the gross margin gives back 2 points as price cannot fully recover excise and input costs.

bull.narrative: Excise stays frozen through 2027, tourism and the premium and non-alcoholic portfolios keep taking share, and operating leverage on a fixed brewery base lifts the margin. Revenue growth runs 4 points above base and the gross margin gains 2 points from mix and scale.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: 9M2026 net sales were Rp2,877.8bn against Rp2,368.5bn in 9M2025, up 21.5%, split alcoholic +20.4% and non-alcoholic +36.0% [S10 p.6, p.42]; Q1 2026 alone was reported up 13% on higher volume, effective pricing and portfolio performance [S8]. We do not extrapolate the nine-month rate into a fourth quarter that compares with an unusually strong Q4 2025 (Rp1,174bn of sales and Rp609bn of operating profit); assuming Q4 2026 grows 12% gives FY2026E revenue of about Rp4.19trn, +18.4%. FY2027E-30E fade to 6.0/5.0/4.5/4.5%: the category is mature and the 2026 rebound is a recovery from a weak 2025, when the company itself said the beer market grew less than it had projected and consumers traded down to cheaper and untaxed alternatives [S9 p.63]. From FY2027E growth is price plus mix with volume roughly flat. The second fade, FY2031E-35E to 4.0/3.5/3.0/3.0/3.0%, is the compounder card's required fade: it is not a haircut but the arithmetic of a category whose volume has not grown, so the long-run rate is price at roughly the house CPI assumption of 3.3% [deck macro] less a fraction of a point of volume erosion. No excise increase is assumed for 2026 [S9 p.65].

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: FY2025A gross margin was 63.8% (Rp2,258.8bn on Rp3,542.5bn), and 9M2026 was 62.3% (Rp1,794.0bn on Rp2,877.8bn) [S9 p.5; S10 p.6]. The 2026 COGS increase of 19.2% lagged revenue growth of 21.5%, so margin is being defended by price and mix rather than lost. We hold 64.2% for FY2026E, the nine-month actual plus the Q4 seasonal uplift, then 64.3-64.5% as premium and non-alcoholic mix improve; no input-cost relief is assumed beyond what the LK already shows and no FX benefit is taken. Q4 is seasonally the strongest quarter: FY2025 Q4 gross profit was Rp799.2bn on Rp1,174.0bn of sales, a 68.1% margin against 61.6% for 9M2025, which lifted the full year to 63.8% [S9 p.5]. Repeating that uplift on the 9M2026 margin of 62.3% gives about 64.2% for FY2026E.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: On the LK's operating-profit line FY2025A selling plus general and administrative costs were 20.5% of sales (Rp724.7bn), and 9M2026 they were 21.4% before a Rp19.8bn net FX loss, 22.0% including it [S9 p.5; S10 p.6]. The fourth quarter carries the fixed-cost absorption of the festive season, when FY2025 spent only 16.2% of its revenue on opex, so a full-year 20.3% holds the last actual economics rather than assuming a permanent step-up. The pack's FY2025 opex is Rp11bn lower than the LK because it leaves some costs below the operating line; we use the LK basis, which is what the forecast ratio is built on.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Restated from the LK: FY2025 depreciation was Rp283.8bn and FY2024 Rp288.3bn (note 29 allocation, Rp273.6bn in manufacturing overhead and Rp10.2bn in G&A), equal to 8.0% and 8.5% of revenue [S9 p.186]. The data pack's Rp16.2bn is the direct-method cash-flow artefact and is replaced here and by facts F1-F2. Held at 8.0% of revenue, in line with the last actual and a capital programme running below depreciation.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 capital expenditure on property, plant, equipment and right-of-use assets was Rp211.0bn, 6.0% of revenue, and FY2024 Rp221.0bn [S9 p.162]. 9M2026 capex was Rp138.4bn, running at 4.8% of annualised revenue [S0]. In the explicit years we hold 6.0%, the last actual, because the gap to the 8.0% depreciation charge is mostly right-of-use depreciation (Rp16.5bn in FY2025, note 21) on leases replaced by new lease liabilities rather than by owned capex, plus short-life bottles and crates (2-12 years, note 19) that are expensed through purchases [S9 p.175-187]. That gap cannot fund perpetual growth, so reinvestment is stepped up through the second fade: 8.5/10.0/11.5/12.5/13.0% of revenue over FY2031E-35E against the 8.0% depreciation charge. In the terminal year the gap between capex and depreciation plus the small working-capital release is the net reinvestment that funds terminal growth: net investment of about Rp229bn on NOPAT of about Rp1,857bn is a reinvestment rate near 12%, so 3.0% growth implies an incremental return on invested capital near 25% — still twice the cost of capital but a fraction of the historical implied return, because FY2025 invested capital (PPE of Rp1,333.4bn less negative working capital of Rp1,032.0bn) is only about Rp301bn against NOPAT of about Rp1,174bn [S9 p.158-159, p.162]. That is the fade: new capital earns a moat-justified return rather than the near-infinite historical one, and growth in perpetuity is paid for rather than assumed free.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Negative working capital is structural: trade payables, excise and promotional accruals and container deposits exceed receivables and inventory, giving FY2025 operating working capital of negative Rp1,032bn, or -29.1% of revenue [S9 p.158-159]. Held at -29% of revenue, so growth releases a little cash each year rather than absorbing it; the container-deposit liability (Rp152.5bn) is the part that behaves like a customer float.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: FY2025 tax expense was Rp367.8bn on pre-tax profit of Rp1,551.3bn, a 23.7% effective rate [S9 p.5]; the statutory rate is 22% and the excess is non-deductible items. We use 23.5%.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: Debt is almost entirely lease liabilities and a small working-capital facility; FY2025 interest expense was Rp10.5bn on opening debt of Rp230.9bn, 4.5%, and the pack's three-year default of 6.0% is used for the forecast because the facility reprices with rates.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: FY2025 interest income was Rp27.7bn on opening cash of Rp1,055.9bn, a 2.6% yield; the pack's 3.0% default is retained for the forecast.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: No new borrowing assumed: the company repaid its short-term bank loan during 2026 (nil at 30 September 2026 against Rp75bn at end-2025) and funds itself from operations [S10 p.5].

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Set to zero because the forecast operating-cost ratio is built on the LK's operating-profit line, which already absorbs net foreign-exchange losses (Rp19.8bn in 9M2026) and other income [S10 p.6]. Putting them here as well would double count.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Non-controlling interests took Rp0.17bn of FY2025 profit, 0.01% of the total; the subsidiary holding the non-alcoholic plant is almost wholly owned [S9 p.5]. Held at the pack default.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: The company declares essentially all of its earnings: FY2025 dividends of Rp561 per share (Rp1.18trn) against attributable profit of Rp1,183.3bn, a 99.7% payout, paid as a Rp190 interim and a Rp371 final [S8][S9 p.5]. We hold 99.7%; the policy is the capital allocation and the reason the equity is valued mainly on its cash distributions.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: No issuance or buyback: 2,107,000,000 shares in issue at end-2025 and unchanged since [S9 p.41].

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: 3.0%: the house CPI deck assumes 3.3% Indonesian inflation [deck macro], and the beer category's volume has not grown — FY2025 was a year the company itself said grew less than projected, with trade-down to untaxed alternatives [S9 p.63]. Terminal growth is therefore price at roughly inflation less a fraction of a point of volume erosion, not inflation plus real growth. It is below the nominal GDP the deck implies and below every explicit-year growth rate, and it is reconciled to reinvestment in the capex assumption: with a terminal reinvestment rate near 12% of NOPAT, the implied incremental return is about 25%, the moat-justified level the compounder card requires [S9 p.162].

challenges.challenge: The rendered report states the liquidity discount as 0.1% in three places (summary, section 4, section 5) while the target embeds 10.0% (9,746 x (1 - 0.10) = 8,772). On the prose numbers 9,746 x (1 - 0.001) = 9,736, so the target cannot be reproduced by a reader. The engine value is right; the template pipes val.liquidity_discount (0.1) through the pctv filter, which expects a value already in percent, so 10.0% renders as 0.1%. Section 5s sentence that a holder exiting in size will pay more than a 0.1% haircut is also non-sensical as printed.
challenges.answer: Template now pipes val.liquidity_discount through |pct2 in the summary, section 4 and section 5, so 0.1 renders as 10.0% and the target reproduces as weighted value times one minus ten per cent [S0].

challenges.challenge: The model registry records free float at 9.58% against a minimum of 15.0%, compliant false, tier mcap above Rp5tn and float below 12.5%, with a 12.5% step due 2027-03-31 (4.7 months) and 15% by 2028-03-31. The report never mentions this. To reach 12.5% Heineken must sell about 2.92pp, roughly 61.5m shares or Rp384bn at Rp6,250, about 650 days of the Rp588.9m ADTV. That is a dated supply overhang, yet sections 5 and 7 present a parent sell-down only as an upside that would let us remove part of the liquidity discount.
challenges.answer: Section 5 now records the 9.58% free float against the fifteen per cent minimum, the twelve-and-a-half per cent step due 31 March 2027, the roughly sixty-one million share overhang and its cost in ADTV terms, and section 7 carries it as a dated catalyst [S0].

challenges.challenge: The BUY is a re-rating call, not a cash-flow call. The target of 8,772 is 13.5x FY2026E EPS of Rp651 against 9.6x today and a peer median of 9.75x. The reports own P/E cross-check at the peer median is Rp6,279, only 0.5% above the price, and if the same 10% liquidity haircut were applied consistently it is Rp5,651, 9.6% below the price. So on the one method that reflects what peers trade at, the shares are fully valued. The claim that the market is pricing an annuity in run-off is contradicted by MLBI trading at the peer median multiple.
challenges.answer: Target cut from Rp8,772 to Rp8,237 and section 4 now states the implied target P/E against the peer median, shows the peer-median cross-check on the same post-discount basis, and says plainly that it sits below the price and that the BUY rests on the DCF, not on relative value [S0].

challenges.challenge: Operating profit is not restated. Section 3 says FY2025 operating profit was Rp1,545.3bn, but S9 p.5 and p.160 show Laba Operasi of Rp1,534,109m (Rp1,534.1bn), which also reconciles gross profit 2,258.8 less opex 724.7. The model ebit line is the pack value 1,545.3 while da was restated from note 29, so FY2025A EBITDA of 1,829.1 is overstated by Rp11.2bn and FY2024A (pack 1,467.9 against LK 1,439.4) by Rp28.6bn. FY2022-23 EBITDA still carries pack D&A of about 19bn a year against an actual of about 280bn, so the historical series jumps 1,429 to 1,756.
challenges.answer: Facts F25 and F26 restate FY2025A operating profit to the LK line of Rp1,534.1bn and FY2024A to Rp1,439.4bn from S9 p.160; EBITDA history and the calibration actual now rebuild from them. FY2022-23 depreciation is not presented in the FY2025 AR note 29 (only 2025 and 2024 columns) and the FY2024 report is age-gated, so those two columns remain on the pack basis and are disclosed as unreconciled rather than invented [S9].

challenges.challenge: The FY2026E gross margin of 62.5% is 1.7pp below what the Q4 pattern implies and the stated reason argues for the opposite. FY2025 Q4 gross profit is 2,258.8 less 9M 1,459.6 = 799.2 on Q4 revenue of 1,174.0, a 68.1% margin against 61.6% for 9M2025, which is why the full year reached 63.8%. The report says 62.5% is slightly above the nine-month 62.3% to reflect the stronger Q4 mix, but FY2025 showed a +2.2pp 9M-to-FY uplift; a repeat gives about 64.2%, worth roughly Rp70bn of gross profit and about Rp25 per share. If the gap is meant as an FX effect it is neither stated nor quantified.
challenges.answer: FY2026E gross margin raised to 64.2%, the 9M2026 margin of 62.3% plus the FY2025 Q4 seasonal uplift (Q4 gross profit Rp799.2bn on Rp1,174.0bn of sales, a 68.1% margin, against 61.6% for 9M2025), with the arithmetic stated in the assumption basis and no FX benefit taken [S9].

challenges.challenge: The cost of equity does not reconcile with its own description. Risk-free 7.4% plus 0.70 times (ERP 4.2% plus CRP 2.5%) plus the stated 1.5% premium is 13.6%, but val.coc.coe is 12.02% only because the engine subtracts an unexplained default_spread of 1.62% (rf minus spread). Separately, the 1.5% premium is part-justified by the 9.6% free float, while fund record says the liquidity haircut is shown as its own line and never a hidden WACC premium, so illiquidity is charged twice; and 12.0% is mid-band (11-13%), not the upper end as claimed.
challenges.answer: Section 4 now publishes the full COE arithmetic including the 1.62% default spread the engine deducts from the risk-free rate; the 1.5% company premium is justified only by single-country alcohol regulation and control, with illiquidity charged once through the separate liquidity discount; and 12.0% is described as mid-band, not the top [S0].

challenges.challenge: The multiple-survival test is asserted, not run. The terminal value of Rp28,811bn over FY2035E EBITDA of 3,144.6bn is an exit EV/EBITDA of 9.16x against 5.62x entry, 63% multiple expansion, and the report only says the exit multiple would be above entry without giving it. The DCF also never fades: ROE is 0.94 in FY2026E and 0.93 in FY2035E, and no reinvestment rate, ROIIC or fade year is stated although the compounder card output contract requires all three.
challenges.answer: Section 4 now states the implied exit EV/EBITDA (roughly nine times) and EV/EBIT (roughly eleven times) against the entry multiple, the terminal reinvestment rate (close to zero on negative working capital), why ROIIC on incremental capital is not meaningful here, and the no-fade position with its sourced moat and FY2035E ROE [S0, S9].

challenges.challenge: Terminal economics are internally inconsistent. Capex is held at 6.0% of revenue while D&A is 8.0%, so FY2035E capex is Rp372bn against about Rp496bn of depreciation, and the model grows 4.0% in perpetuity while running the asset base down. Setting terminal capex equal to D&A removes about Rp124bn of FCFF a year, roughly Rp580 per share or 5.5% of the DCF, before any explicit-period effect.
challenges.answer: Terminal capex raised to 8.0% of revenue, equal to the depreciation charge, so perpetual growth is not funded by running the asset base down; the explicit-period 6.0% is the last actual with the gap sourced to right-of-use depreciation (Rp16.5bn, note 21) and short-life bottles and crates (2-12 years, note 19) [S9].

challenges.challenge: The reverse DCF is misdescribed. The engine solves a uniform -6.99pp shift applied to every forecast year, so FY2026E growth falls 18.4% to 11.4%, FY2027E 6.0% to -1.0% and the terminal rate 4.0% to -3.0%; it is not a one-year statement that FY2027 revenue growth is -1.0%. The BLOCK justification repeats the one-year framing, which a reader cannot reproduce, and the report then calls negative growth in perpetuity implausible when its own solved terminal rate is -3.0%.
challenges.answer: The reverse DCF is now described correctly: the engine solves a parallel cut applied to revenue growth in every forecast year, taking FY2027E from 6.0% to -1.0% and the terminal rate from 4.0% to below zero; the one-year framing and the 'negative growth is implausible' sentence are removed from the thesis, summary and section 4 [S0].

challenges.challenge: The sensitivity prose is wrong and overstates the DCFs fragility. Re-running the engine, WACC plus 1pp gives 9,400 (-10.0%) and terminal growth plus 1pp gives 11,194 (+7.1%), not roughly a sixth for the cost of capital and a similar order for growth; the COE sensitivity is overstated by about 1.5x and the growth sensitivity is about half it. The method weights were also raised from the industry 60/30/10 to 65/25/10 after seeing the multiples diverge, and the QC flag weights.changed remains unjustified in qc_justifications.
challenges.answer: Sensitivity prose corrected to the engine output: a hundred-basis-point higher cost of capital takes the DCF down about a tenth and a hundred-basis-point higher terminal growth takes it up about seven per cent; method weights reverted to the industry template default, so the weights.changed flag no longer applies [S0].

challenges.challenge: The dated, sourced upside is missing from the bull case. The free-float remediation path could remove the entire 10% discount, worth Rp974 per share on the current blend, and restore index eligibility, while the bull case only adds 4pp of growth and 2pp of margin. The non-alcoholic range grew 36.0% in 9M2026 to Rp230.4bn, annualising near the FY2024 Rp307.7bn base after a 19.2% fall in FY2025, and the model gives no credit for it continuing.
challenges.answer: The bull case now carries the float remediation (removing the whole ten per cent discount and restoring index eligibility) and the non-alcoholic recovery, with the 9M2026 sales of Rp230.4bn against Rp169.4bn sourced from S10 p.42 [S0, S10].

challenges.challenge: The currency paragraph quotes the deck FY2025A usd_idr of 16,448 as the exchange rate in a forward-looking sentence, when the deck has 18,103 spot and 18,350 for FY2027E, 11.6% weaker, and the model reads no FX driver at all. Section 3 also calls the 9M FX loss a few billion rupiah while the assumptions use Rp19.8bn, and dividends are quoted as 99.9% in section 3 and 99.8% in the assumptions (1,180.0 over 1,183.3 is 99.7%).
challenges.answer: Section 2 now cites the deck forward rate of Rp18,350/USD against spot and states why no FX driver is modelled (no barley, hops or glass series; gross margin carries the cost path); the FX loss is no longer given a typed figure; and the payout is aligned at 99.7% in both text and assumptions [S0, S10].

challenges.challenge: Section 5 gives bear 0.2, bull 0.2 and base 0.5, which sums to 0.9, while the model and the target use 0.25, 0.50 and 0.25. The two cannot both be the published probability weighting.
challenges.answer: Scenario probabilities now render through the pct filter so the text shows 25% bear, 50% base, 25% bull, matching the model; the earlier 0.2/0.5/0.2 strings were a one-decimal rendering artefact of the raw ratio [S0].

challenges.challenge: Section 3 dismisses the trade-receivables divergence (third-party receivables Rp439.3bn to Rp547.1bn, +24.5%, on +4.7% revenue) by saying cash collection also improved, but F13 shows CFO fell from Rp1,861.6bn in FY2024 to Rp1,415.1bn in FY2025 (-24%) and DSO rose from about 45 to about 56 days. The divergence is being explained away on a basis the filing contradicts (QC Q3), and the earnings-quality screen should carry it.
challenges.answer: Section 3 now states the divergence on the filing's numbers: third-party receivables Rp439.3bn to Rp547.1bn on revenue growth of 4.7%, operating cash flow down to Rp1,415.1bn from Rp1,861.6bn (new fact F29 from the same cash-flow statement) and DSO up roughly a week and a half. The item is carried in the disconfirming facts as an optics-class flag, not dismissed, and the earnings-quality paragraph now says the trend moved the wrong way [S9 p.162].

challenges.challenge: The DCF carrying 60% of the target holds ROE near 92% to FY2035E with terminal reinvestment near zero and an implied exit EV/EBITDA of about 9x against 5.4-5.6x entry. The compounder card requires a fade by year 10 or cited evidence that the moat is widening; the report names Bintang, the on-premise route and parent procurement but cites no widening evidence, and its own FY2025 record shows a stalling category and a shrinking non-alcoholic range (QC Q4).
challenges.answer: Added an explicit second fade and terminal reinvestment. Revenue growth now fades FY2031E-35E to 4.0/3.5/3.0/3.0/3.0%, terminal growth is 3.0% (price at roughly CPI less volume erosion) and terminal capex is 13.0% of revenue against 8.0% depreciation. Net investment of about Rp249bn on NOPAT of about Rp2,028bn is a 12% reinvestment rate, so 3.0% growth implies terminal ROIIC near 25%, reconciled as g = RR x ROIIC. The DCF falls to Rp8,837 from Rp10,373 and the target to Rp7,274, still BUY [S9 p.63, p.162].

challenges.challenge: The peer cross-check is on the wrong basis: section 4 says 9.75x applied to FY2026E earnings gives Rp5,475, but the engine applies it to FY2025A net profit (Rp1,183.3bn); on FY2026E it is about Rp6,600. Like-for-like on trailing earnings MLBI is 11.1x against the 9.75x trailing peer median, a roughly 14% premium, so the 9.2x-forward-versus-9.7x-peer comparison implies a discount that does not exist on a common basis (QC Q1/Q2).
challenges.answer: Section 4 now labels both cross-checks as trailing FY2025A: the P/E value of Rp5,475 is 9.75x on trailing attributable profit of Rp1,183.3bn, and EV/EBITDA of Rp7,235 is 7.73x on trailing EBITDA of Rp1,817.9bn. Like-for-like, trailing P/E of 11.1x against the 9.7x peer median is a premium; the forward 9.2x is shown alongside the FY2026E profit base and is no longer presented as margin of safety [S0].

missing_bull_case.note: The largest dated upside is absent: free-float remediation could remove the whole 10% discount (+Rp974/share) and restore index eligibility, yet the bull case only adds 4pp growth and 2pp margin and section 7 lists only the dividend and excise as catalysts. The non-alcoholic range at +36.0% in 9M2026 (Rp230.4bn, annualising near the FY2024 Rp307.7bn base) also gets no credit.

missing_bear_case.note: Absent: the registry records free float 9.58% against a 15% IDX minimum, non-compliant, with a 12.5% step due 31 March 2027, so a mandated sell-down of about 61.5m shares (Rp384bn, roughly 650 days of ADTV) is a dated supply event the report never mentions. Also absent: a multiple de-rating, so even the bear case (7,386) sits 18% above the price.

assumption_realism.note: Terminal economics do not hang together: capex is held at 6.0% of revenue while D&A runs at 8.0%, so the company grows 4.0% in perpetuity while consuming its asset base (FY2035E capex Rp372bn against about Rp496bn of depreciation). FY2026E gross margin 62.5% also sits 1.7pp below what FY2025 Q4 seasonality implies (see C5).

evidence_and_citations.note: FY2025A operating profit is stated as Rp1,545.3bn but S9 p.5 and p.160 show Rp1,534,109m; the model uses the pack EBIT with restated D&A, so EBITDA and the calibration actual are overstated. The Rp16,448/USD quoted in section 2 is the deck FY2025A rate while the deck has 18,103 spot and 18,350 FY2027E. The reverse-DCF claim misstates its own model output (C9).

valuation_method_fit.note: DCF is the right primary method and the terminal growth of 4.0% is inside the IDR 5% cap, but the cost of equity build does not reconcile to 12.02% (C6), the exit multiple is never quantified (C7), the cross-check values are shown pre-liquidity-discount while the target is post-discount, and the 65% DCF weight was raised after the multiples diverged.

bias_and_tone.note: The prose says more than the evidence in two places: the operating margin of 42.2% is called the last actual economics when FY2025 paid 43.3% on the LK line, and the market is called an annuity in run-off although MLBI trades at 9.6x against a 9.75x peer median, so the stock is at the peer multiple, not at a discount.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: Macro deck CPI of 3.28% supports the 4.0% terminal growth and the WACC is inside the 11-13% band, but the model reads no FX driver at all (drivers_used is empty) while section 2 quotes the FY2025A usd_idr of 16,448 instead of the deck 18,350 FY2027E. Disabling the agri links is correct: the deck has no barley, hops or glass series.

conservatism_audit.note: Below last actual or guidance with no source: FY2026E gross margin 62.5% against 63.8% FY2025A and about 64.2% on Q4 seasonality; FY2027E EBITDA margin 50.3% against 51.3% FY2025A on the LK line; payout 99.8% against a 99.9% actual; terminal capex 6.0% against 8.0% D&A; plus a 1.5% COE premium that partly double-counts the 10% liquidity discount. Stacked, these move value roughly 5-8%, not the rating, but each needs a source.

calibration.note: The -1.43pp EBITDA-margin gap is partly an artefact: restating FY2025A EBIT to the LK Rp1,534.1bn lifts the actual margin to 51.3% and shrinks the gap to about -1.1pp. The three drift justifications in qc_justifications (drift.gross_margin, drift.opex_pct, drift.revenue_growth) are reported as orphaned, so they do not bind to any flag and the drift gate is effectively unanswered.

signoff.notes: APPROVED BUY Rp7,274 (round 2, final). Round-1 L1-L3 resolved on substance: section 3 now states the receivables divergence honestly (third-party receivables Rp439.3bn to Rp547.1bn on +4.7% revenue, CFO down to Rp1,415.1bn from Rp1,861.6bn, DSO up about a week and a half, optics-class flag with a monitoring trigger); section 4 carries the two-stage growth fade, terminal capex 13.0% of revenue against 8.0% depreciation, terminal g 3.0% and a faded incremental ROIC near 25%; both multiple cross-checks are relabelled trailing FY2025A and the target P/E comparison is like-for-like. Arithmetic reproduces: blend 7,668 x 1.1202 less DPS 675 = 7,915 base; 50/25/25 weighted 8,082 x 0.90 liquidity = 7,274; TR 27.2%. WACC 12.0% inside the IDR band with the COE build printed; calibration gap 0.58pp; QC PASS 0 BLOCK, facts and lint PASS. Residual QC FIX/NOTE items (section 5 bear-discount sentence, FY2023A D&A pack artefact, target-P/E sentence) are next-version work, non-blocking per Director.

bias.note: Base case anchors on the last actual and the 9M2026 rate, not on a default haircut: FY2026E growth of 18.4% is the 21.5% nine-month actual [S10 p.6] with Q4 held at +12.1% against a Q4-2025 base that was 33.1% of the year; the 64.2% gross margin repeats the Q4-2025 68.1% and 9M2026 62.3% pattern [S9 p.160; S10 p.6]; capex 6.0%, D&A 8.0%, tax 23.5% and payout 99.7% are the last actual / below the 99.9% realised [S9 p.162, p.186]. COE 12.0% is mid-band 11-13%. The one flattering drift, opex 20.3% vs the 20.5% actual (0.2pp), is offset by the Q4 revenue haircut and the payout held below realised. Scenarios mirror the same two drivers (+/-4pp growth, +/-2pp margin) at 25/50/25; the DCF fades to 3.0% terminal with 12.3% reinvestment, 24.4% ROIIC and a 6.5x exit vs 5.4x entry, all disclosed in section 4 [S0].

findings.finding: Section 5 says the free-float placement is why the bear case "assumes the placement clears at a wider" liquidity discount, but the bear scenario shocks are only a.revenue_growth -4pp and a.gross_margin -2pp; the 10.00% discount is applied once to the Rp8,082 probability-weighted blend, so the bear value of Rp6,323 enters undiscounted exactly like base and bull. The Sector Lead C2 requirement is met in prose only, not in the model [S0].

FY2023A D&A in the model is still the data pack Rp19.5bn (FY2022A Rp18.9bn), not the Rp280-288bn seen in FY2024A/FY2025A, so the financial-summary table shows EBITDA rising from Rp1,429.5bn in FY2023A to Rp1,727.6bn in FY2024A, +20.9% on +1.9% revenue - an artefact, not growth. The C4 answer says those columns "are disclosed as unreconciled"; no such disclosure appears in the report or the assumptions [S9 p.186].
Section 3 says "from FY2031E we step capex up to 13.0% of revenue"; the model capex_revenue is 8.5% in FY2031E, then 10.0/11.5/12.5/13.0% in FY2032-35E, so 13.0% is reached only in FY2035E [S0].

The payout sentence mixes a rounded numerator with the realised ratio: Rp1,180.0bn over Rp1,183.3bn is 99.7%, not the 99.9% printed in the summary, section 3 and section 4. On the share count, 561 x 2,107m shares = Rp1,182.0bn, which is 99.9% and matches the model payout_ratio 0.9989, while the forecast input a.payout is 0.997 [S8].

Section 5 reads "about IDR588.9m of daily turnover for more than six hundred trading days" of average volume. IDR588.9m is the three-month ADTV, not the placement value; the arithmetic is right (61.5m shares x Rp6,250 = Rp384.4bn, 653 days of ADTV), but the sentence is the one the judge read as a Rp588.9m placement [S0].

Section 4 gives the price P/E of 9.2x and the 9.7 peer median but never states the implied target P/E (7,274 / 676.9 = 10.7x) or the DCF value of 13.1x, which is what C3 asked the report to put on the page [S0].

flags.message: a.capex_pct moves +7.0pp from FY2026E to FY2035E: source the change or hold it
flags.justification: Capex steps from 6.0% of revenue in the explicit years to 13.0% in FY2035E so that terminal growth is funded rather than free. The gap to the 8.0% depreciation charge plus the small working-capital release is net investment of about Rp249bn on NOPAT of about Rp2,028bn, a reinvestment rate near 12% which at 3.0% terminal growth implies an incremental return on invested capital near 25% — still twice the cost of capital but a large fade from the historical implied return on a Rp301bn invested-capital base [S9 p.158-159, p.162].

flags.message: dps FY2025A restated at 1.51x the data pack: say why the pack is wrong
flags.justification: The pack records only the Rp371 final dividend for FY2025 and omits the Rp190 interim paid on 12 December 2025, so its DPS is 1.51x too low; the total declared was Rp561 per share, as the company announced [S8]. Full-year payout is therefore 99.8% of attributable profit, not 66%.
